Memory and HBM

SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make nearly all high bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked memory beside AI chips. SK hynix took 63.2 percent of HBM revenue in 2025.

In plain terms

High bandwidth memory, or HBM, is where an AI chip keeps the numbers it is working on, and it is built to hand them over fast. A memory maker etches tiny holes into each memory wafer, fills them with copper and grinds the wafer until the copper shows through its back. It tests each of the wafer's chips and stacks up to sixteen good ones into a cube, with every layer wired to the ones below. The cube then sits beside the processor, the chip that does the calculating. Stacking is the hard part because each chip is ground thinner than a human hair and the finished cube has to stay within a height limit of less than a millimeter. One chip that fails after stacking can scrap the whole cube. Only SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make HBM in volume. One US export rule covers HBM from all three, including the two based in South Korea.

In short

US-based Micron went from 5.8 percent of HBM revenue in 2024 to 23.1 percent in the first quarter of 2026, according to IDC figures in SK hynix's US prospectus[1]. Over the same period, Samsung's share fell from 37.8 percent to 20.5 percent[1].

Since December 2024, a US license has been required, unless an exception applies, to export to China any HBM moving more than 2 GB per second per square millimeter of its area[2]. The Institute for Progress reported in October 2025 that China's CXMT planned to produce HBM3 in 2026[3]. Even so, working from TrendForce's estimate of world HBM shipments, the institute projected that producers outside China would make 70 times as much HBM as China in 2026[3]. In June 2026 SemiAnalysis judged that CXMT was still struggling to stabilize supply of eight-high HBM3[4].

An AI accelerator moves numbers from memory to its arithmetic units and back. The US export control office wrote in December 2024 that a processor cannot reach its full capabilities unless its memory capacity and bandwidth rise with its speed[2].

Why substitution is slow
SK hynix says only a few firms have the expertise and resources to design, make and package memory chips[1]. It says HBM also needs advanced processes such as packaging with through-silicon vias (TSVs), the copper-filled holes that link the layers, and must pass customers' rigorous testing and approval[1].
Where China stands

The Institute for Progress estimated in October 2025 that China would make virtually no HBM that year[3]. Huawei said in September 2025 that its Ascend 950 chips would use two HBM designs of its own, without saying who would manufacture the memory[6].

Where the US stands

Micron is the only American HBM maker[1]. As of October 2026, License Exception HBM lets US and allied exporters ship HBM below 3.3 GB per second per square millimeter without a license, including to China when the chip designer buys it directly and it goes straight to the packaging site[7].

How it works

Each layer in the cube is a DRAM chip, the ordinary kind of computer memory. Each layer is ground thin and bonded to the one below through tiny metal bumps called microbumps. The whole stack sits on a base die, a chip that manages it. The copper-filled holes are called through-silicon vias, or TSVs. They let a signal reach any layer without a wire running around the outside.

An HBM3E cube has a 1,024-bit interface, meaning it exchanges data with the processor over 1,024 wires at once[8]. That is sixteen times wider than a standard DDR5 memory module, the memory stick in a PC[8]. HBM4 doubles that to 2,048 wires[9]. Ordinary memory cannot be made that wide, because the pins would not fit on a circuit board. The stack can, since its wires run down through the TSVs and across a silicon interposer to the processor beside it, with no board in the way[8]. The interposer is a slice of silicon carrying fine wiring, set under both the memory and the processor (see Advanced packaging).

A chip needs the width most when it answers a prompt. Training reuses each stored number across a huge multiplication, so a chip can fetch little and compute a lot. But to generate one word of an answer, the chip reads the whole model from memory, plus the whole record of the conversation so far. Then it does a little arithmetic and waits for the next read. That record grows with the length of the conversation and the number of users served at once. So memory size and speed usually set how many people one chip can serve.

HBM3E

Micron's HBM3E comes in two sizes, 24 GB with eight chips stacked and 36 GB with twelve[10].

HBM4

All three HBM makers run their HBM4 faster than the 8 Gb/s per pin in the industry standard. The standards body JEDEC published JESD270-4 in April 2025, setting the 2,048-bit interface and 2 TB/s per stack at 8 Gb/s per pin[9]. SK hynix says it was first to complete HBM4 development, in September 2025, at over 10 Gb/s per pin[11]. Samsung says it began mass production and shipped the first commercial HBM4 in February 2026, at 11.7 Gb/s per pin, with a 4 nm logic base die[12]. Micron's parts run above 11 Gb/s for more than 2.8 TB/s per stack[13]. Micron says it began volume production of its 36 GB twelve-high HBM4 in fiscal 2026 and expects to ramp volume of HBM4E, the next generation, in calendar 2027[14].

Through HBM3E, SK hynix made its own base dies, the chips at the bottom of each stack[15]. For HBM4 it chose TSMC's advanced logic process, so the base die can hold more functions[15]. As a result, TSMC, which does not make HBM, makes the base die for SK hynix's HBM4.

How a stack is built

  • Etch and thin. Etch vertical holes, the through-silicon vias, into a memory wafer, fill them with copper, then grind the wafer from behind until the copper comes through.
  • Stack and join. Thermocompression bonding joins the chips through metal bumps under heat and pressure, and it comes in several types, such as TC-NCF and MR-MUF, short for mass reflow molded underfill[17]. SK hynix uses its own version, Advanced MR-MUF, which stacks the chips, injects a liquid protective material between them and hardens it[11]. SK hynix says the process controls warping and dissipates heat well[11]. Samsung said in February 2024 that its twelve-high HBM3E uses TC-NCF, thermocompression with a thin non-conductive film between the chips[18]. Samsung expected TC-NCF to help limit warping as chips get thinner[18].
  • Stay under the height limit. The package specification for HBM4 raised the height allowed for a finished cube from 720 micrometers to 775, still under a millimeter[17].

Hybrid bonding is the next step, but it is not ready. It would join the chips copper to copper and insulator to insulator, with no solder and no filler[17]. In chip packaging generally, microbumps sit about 20 micrometers apart, and hybrid bonds can sit less than 1 micrometer apart[17]. A tech note on SK hynix's newsroom says full-scale adoption in HBM is most likely at HBM4E or HBM5, where stacks are projected to pass twenty layers[17]. Taller stacks trap more heat, and removing it becomes a major challenge at 16 to 20 layers[17]. The same tech note says hybrid bonding manages that heat more efficiently[17].

Who makes it

Three firms took more than 90 percent of the revenue from ordinary computer memory, or DRAM, in the first quarter of 2026, according to IDC figures in SK hynix's US prospectus[1]. HBM comes from the same three, SK hynix, Samsung and Micron[1]. No other company has both leading-edge DRAM and a stacking line of its own. SK hynix says only a few firms have the expertise and resources to design, make and package memory chips[1]. It says HBM also needs advanced production processes, such as TSV packaging, and must pass the rigorous testing and approval processes its customers set[1].

SK hynix says it was the first company to mass-produce several generations of HBM, including HBM3 and HBM3E[1].

SK hynix and Micron are both adding HBM capacity. SK hynix broke ground in August 2026 on an advanced packaging plant in West Lafayette, Indiana, an investment of over $4 billion[19]. Micron is modernizing and expanding its DRAM and HBM production capacity in Taiwan[14]. It has also broken ground on an HBM advanced packaging plant in Singapore to expand its packaging capacity from early 2027[14].

SK hynix led HBM revenue in 2024, in 2025 and in the first quarter of 2026, and in that quarter Micron passed Samsung for second place. In 2024 SK hynix took 56.4 percent, Samsung 37.8 and Micron 5.8[1]. In 2025 the three took 63.2, 19.3 and 17.4 percent[1]. In the first quarter of 2026 they stood at 56.4, 20.5 and 23.1 percent, which put SK hynix back at its 2024 share[1]. The split is public because SK hynix registered shares in the United States, and its US prospectus credits the research firm IDC[1].

As HBM grows, memory makers have less factory capacity left for traditional DRAM. In December 2025 Micron put the HBM market at about $35 billion in 2025 and forecast that it would reach around $100 billion in 2028[5]. Micron says HBM needs more wafers than traditional DRAM, the kind used in PCs and phones, to make the same number of bits[14]. SK hynix says the industry's shift of production capacity to HBM has left traditional DRAM undersupplied[1]. The shortage, it says, helped drive a significant price recovery for that DRAM from the third quarter of 2025[1].

The chokepoint

The leading accelerators made outside China use HBM from SK hynix, Samsung or Micron. Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 rack carries 20 TB of HBM3E at up to 576 TB/s[20]. Each Nvidia Rubin GPU carries up to 288 GB of HBM4 at up to 22 TB/s[21]. AMD's MI355X carries 288 GB of HBM3E at 8 TB/s[22].

A US export rule of December 2024 covers every HBM stack that was in production when it was published. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the US export control office, published the rule on 5 December 2024[2]. It added an export classification, ECCN 3A090.c, for "High bandwidth memory (HBM) having a 'memory bandwidth density' greater than 2 gigabytes per second per square millimeter"[2]. Its technical note defines that density as the memory bandwidth in gigabytes per second divided by the area of the package or stack in square millimeters[2]. The rule also covers stacks made outside the United States, through a foreign direct product rule, which applies US controls to goods made abroad with American technology[2]. BIS stated in the rule that all HBM stacks then in production exceeded that threshold[2].

BIS reviews license applications to ship controlled HBM to Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination such as China according to where the buyer is headquartered[23]. It presumes it will deny a license when the buyer or its ultimate parent is headquartered in one of those places, and presumes approval otherwise[23].

Two provisions narrow the control. License Exception HBM, at 15 CFR 740.25, applies to exporters headquartered in the United States or a Country Group A:5 ally[7]. It lets them ship HBM below 3.3 GB per second per square millimeter without a license, including to Macau and Country Group D:5 destinations such as China[7]. HBM sent to those destinations must be bought directly by the designer of the chip it will be packaged into[7]. Every shipment under the exception must go straight to the packaging site[7]. The rule also excludes co-packaged chips that combine HBM and logic and whose main function is processing, which other chip controls may cover instead[2].

The think tank CSIS said in December 2024 that the rules still allowed HBM2, a generation introduced in 2016, to go to China, with limits on who could buy it and what for[24]. It also said Nvidia's H20, whose HBM3 is packaged with the processor, was then still exportable under the performance limits for AI chips[24].

China's strongest DRAM maker, CXMT, was still struggling to make HBM in steady supply by June 2026. In December 2024 CSIS called CXMT one of only two Chinese firms with a credible path to producing advanced HBM, though it did not name the other[24]. The Institute for Progress reported in October 2025 that CXMT was planning to produce HBM3 in 2026[3]. It also estimated that China would make virtually no HBM in 2025[3]. In June 2026 SemiAnalysis judged that CXMT was still struggling to stabilize supply of eight-high HBM3, with even greater challenges at twelve-high[4].

Huawei plans to use HBM of its own design in its Ascend 950 AI chips, but when it announced the designs in September 2025 it did not say who would make the memory[6]. The two designs are called HiBL 1.0 and HiZQ 2.0[6]. Huawei said the 950DT, due in the fourth quarter of 2026, would carry 144 GB of HiZQ 2.0 at 4 TB/s[6].

Review questions

Open a question to see its answer.

What is HBM?

High-bandwidth memory, made of memory chips stacked into a cube beside the processor and wired to pass data fast.

Before stacking, each chip gets holes filled with copper, which wire every layer to the ones below. A stack holds up to sixteen chips. Reread: How it works

Why does an AI chip need such fast memory?

For each word it writes, it reads the whole model from memory.

Memory speed and size usually set how many users one chip can serve. Reread: How it works

Who makes HBM?

SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make nearly all of it.

SK hynix sold 63.2 percent of it in 2025 and Samsung 19.3 percent. A fourth maker would need both the newest DRAM, the kind of memory chip used in PCs and phones, and a line that stacks it. Reread: Who makes it

How much HBM did China make in 2025?

Virtually none, the Institute for Progress estimated in October 2025.

China's strongest DRAM maker, CXMT, was still struggling to make HBM in steady supply by June 2026. A US export rule of December 2024 controls every HBM stack that was in production when the rule was published. Reread: The chokepoint
